n: Once the riot was over, Paul gathered the disciples, encouraged them, said goodbye, and set out for Macedonia.

f.w: departed for to go into Macedonia

n: He traveled through Macedonia, strengthening the churches with much encouragement, and then went on to Greece.

f.g: Here, the province of Achaia, including Corinth.

n: He stayed three months — likely in Corinth, where he probably wrote Romans. Learning of a plot against him, he changed plans and went back overland through Macedonia.
Paul traveled with a group of representatives from various churches — likely carrying the collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem.
These companions went ahead and waited for Paul’s group at Troas.
The “we” returns — Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi. After the Passover season they sailed to Troas in five days and stayed a week.

f.g: The week-long feast following Passover, in spring.

n: On Sunday, the first day of the week, the believers met to “break bread” — the sacrament. Paul, leaving the next day, preached until midnight.

f.w: the first day of the week

n: Many oil lamps burned in the crowded upstairs room, making it warm and stuffy — a detail that helps explain what happened next.

f.g: An upstairs room, often used for gatherings.

n: A young man named Eutychus, sitting in a window, fell asleep during Paul’s long sermon and fell three stories. He was picked up dead.

f.g: A name meaning “fortunate” — fitting, given what follows.

n: Paul went down, lay on him and embraced him, and said, Don’t worry — his life is in him. Like Elijah and Elisha, Paul restored the young man to life.

f.w: fell on him, and embracing him

n: Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, ate, and kept talking until dawn before leaving.
They took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted.
Luke and the others sailed ahead to Assos, while Paul chose to walk there — about 20 miles overland — perhaps wanting time alone.
They picked Paul up at Assos and sailed to Mitylene on the island of Lesbos.
They island-hopped down the coast past Chios and Samos to Miletus. Luke records the voyage like a careful travel diary.

f.g: A port about 30 miles south of Ephesus.

n: Paul skipped Ephesus to avoid delays, hoping to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, about fifty days after Passover.

f.g: Jewish harvest festival, fifty days after Passover.

n: From Miletus he sent for the elders of the Ephesian church to meet him there.
Paul’s farewell speech to the Ephesian elders — the only speech in Acts addressed to Church leaders. He begins by reminding them how he lived among them.
He served the Lord humbly, with tears, enduring trials from plots against him.
He held nothing back that would help them, teaching both in public and in their homes.
His message to Jews and Greeks alike: turn to God in repentance and have faith in Jesus Christ — the first principles of the gospel.

f.w: repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ

n: Now, compelled by the Spirit, Paul was heading to Jerusalem without knowing what would happen there.

f.g: Constrained or compelled by the Spirit.

n: He knew only that the Holy Ghost warned in every city that imprisonment and suffering awaited him.
But none of that would stop him. His life mattered less to him than finishing his mission joyfully and testifying of God’s grace.

f.w: the gospel of the grace of God

n: He told them sadly that they would never see his face again.
He solemnly declared himself free of responsibility for anyone’s spiritual loss — he had done his duty.

f.w: pure from the blood of all men

n: He had not avoided teaching them the whole plan and purpose of God, including the hard parts.
Paul charged the elders to watch over themselves and the flock, which the Holy Ghost had appointed them to shepherd. The Church is precious — bought with Christ’s own blood.

f.g: Greek episkopoi — overseers, the word later rendered “bishops.”

n: He warned that after he left, vicious “wolves” would come in and attack the flock — an early prophecy of apostasy.
Worse, some from their own leadership would twist the truth to gain followers. Latter-day Saints see this as foretelling the Great Apostasy.
So stay alert, and remember how for three years I warned you day and night with tears.
Paul entrusted them to God and his gracious word, which can build them up and give them an inheritance among the sanctified.

f.w: an inheritance among all them which are sanctified

n: He had never wanted anyone’s money or possessions.
His own hands — as a tentmaker — had supported him and his companions.

f.w: these hands have ministered unto my necessities

n: By working hard he set an example of helping the weak. He quotes a saying of Jesus found nowhere in the Gospels: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”

f.w: It is more blessed to give than to receive
f.g: A saying of Jesus preserved only here.

n: When he finished, Paul knelt and prayed with them all.
They all wept openly, hugged him, and kissed him goodbye.
What saddened them most was knowing they would never see him again. They walked him to the ship.
